fields.Front: Name the three main types of constraints in relational databases.
fields.Back: Key constraints, referential integrity constraints, semantic integrity constraints.

fields.Text: The three main types of relational constraints are {{c1::key}} constraints, {{c2::referential integrity}} constraints and {{c3::semantic integrity}} constraints.
A table can have only {{c1::one}} primary key, but it may be made up of {{c2::several attributes}}; it must be {{c3::unique}}.

fields.Front: What does the NOT NULL constraint do for keys?
fields.Back: Forces the user never to leave a key attribute null (empty) for any tuple.

fields.Front: Define referential integrity.
fields.Back: A tuple in one relation that refers to another relation must refer to an existing tuple in that relation (foreign keys may not dangle).

fields.Front: State the two formal rules of referential integrity between FK in R1 and PK in R2.
fields.Back: FK attributes must have the same domain as PK; a value of FK in a tuple of r1(R1) either occurs as a PK value of some tuple in r2(R2) or is null.

fields.Text: A null foreign key {{c1::does not}} violate referential integrity (unless NOT NULL is declared separately).

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is Insert <13,'Gumble','Barney','S7G','M'> into EMPLOYEE valid?
fields.Back: Yes: EmpID 13 is new and department S7G exists.

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is Insert <3,'Simpson','Granpa','Y5J','M'> into EMPLOYEE valid?
fields.Back: No: EmpID 3 already exists (Patty Beuvieau); key/uniqueness constraint violated.

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is Insert <NULL,'Flanders','Ned','Y5J','M'> into EMPLOYEE valid?
fields.Back: No: the primary key is null; entity integrity (NOT NULL) violated.

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is Insert <18,'Flanders','Todd','P68','M'> into EMPLOYEE valid?
fields.Back: No: department P68 does not exist; referential integrity violated.

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is 'Delete employee where EmpID = 4' valid?
fields.Back: Not as stated: employee 4 (Burns) is the manager of department G8H (MgrEmpID = 4), so the delete would leave a dangling reference (referential integrity).

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is 'Delete department where DeptID = S7G' valid?
fields.Back: Not as stated: employees 1, 3 and 12 have DeptID S7G; their foreign keys would dangle.

fields.Front: What three referential actions does DB2 allow on delete, and what does each do?
fields.Back: Cascade: also delete the referencing rows (be careful: it may delete more than you want). Restrict: refuse the delete while referencing rows exist (the instructor calls this 'sort of the default'). Set Null: delete and set the referencing foreign keys to null.

fields.Text: On delete, the three referential-integrity options are {{c1::cascade}} (delete referencing rows too), {{c2::restrict}} (refuse the delete) and {{c3::set null}} (null out the foreign keys).

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is modifying Burns's gender to 'F' valid?
fields.Back: Yes: Sex is neither a key nor a foreign key.

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is modifying Smithers's DeptID from G8H to Y5J valid? To J9J?
fields.Back: To Y5J: yes (Y5J exists). To J9J: no (J9J does not exist; referential integrity).

fields.Front: Lesson 10 tables: is modifying Smithers's EmpID from 2 to 12 valid?
fields.Back: No: EmpID 12 already belongs to Homer Simpson; key constraint violated.

fields.Front: Which constraints can an INSERT violate? A DELETE? A MODIFY?
fields.Back: Insert: key constraints (duplicate/null PK) and referential integrity (FK pointing nowhere, e.g. department P68). Delete: referential integrity (removing a row that other rows reference, e.g. employee 4 who manages G8H). Modify: either, depending on whether a PK, FK or ordinary attribute changes.

fields.Front: Define a state constraint and give the slide examples.
fields.Back: A constraint that a valid database state must satisfy; e.g. hours worked cannot exceed 50; quantity ordered must be greater than 10.

fields.Front: Define a transition constraint and give the slide example.
fields.Back: A constraint on how the database state may change; e.g. salaries can only increase.

fields.Text: 'Hours worked cannot be greater than 50' is a {{c1::state}} constraint; 'salaries can only increase' is a {{c2::transition}} constraint. Both are {{c3::semantic integrity}} constraints.
Semantic integrity constraints are enforced through {{c1::triggers}} and {{c2::assertions}}.
Triggers fire on {{c1::inserts, updates or deletes}}; constraints are checked on {{c2::inserts and updates}}.

fields.Front: Why does 'salaries can only increase' need a trigger rather than a CHECK constraint?
fields.Back: It compares the old and new values (two states); a CHECK such as CHECK (Age >= 18) sees only the row being written, while a trigger can see both OLD and NEW.

fields.Front: What are the objectives of the constraints video?
fields.Back: List key constraints; list referential integrity constraints and tell whether an insert, delete or change will violate them; identify semantic integrity constraints.

fields.Front: What message does Access give when you insert a row whose primary key already exists?
fields.Back: 'The changes you requested to the table were not successful because they would create duplicate values in the index, primary key, or relationship.'

fields.Front: What message does Access give when you leave the primary key empty?
fields.Back: 'You must enter a value': the not-null constraint.

fields.Front: What message does Access give when a foreign key refers to a department that does not exist?
fields.Back: 'You cannot add or change a record because a related record is required in table Department.' (Record just means row.)

fields.Front: What message does Access give when you try to delete employee 4, the manager of Head Office?
fields.Back: 'This record cannot be deleted because the table Department includes related records.'

fields.Front: Give the instructor's plain-language definition of referential integrity.
fields.Back: Your foreign keys have to exist in the table they refer to: if an employee works for S7G there had better be a department S7G, and you cannot make employee 66 a manager if there is no employee 66.

fields.Text: The instructor calls restrict 'sort of the {{c1::default}}'; with set null the DBMS 'doesn't know what to put here' so it puts {{c2::null}} in the referencing rows.

fields.Front: How many records are lost if department S7G is deleted with cascade, and which?
fields.Back: Four: the department row plus employees Bart (1), Patty (3) and Homer (12), who all work in S7G.

fields.Front: How do you enable cascade delete in Access?
fields.Back: Right-click the relationship line and tick Cascade Delete Related Records.

fields.Front: Why does the instructor say to be careful with cascade?
fields.Back: What it does might not be what you want: deleting one department silently deletes every employee in it.

fields.Front: What happened when the instructor deleted the relationships (referential integrity) in Access and retried the modifications?
fields.Back: Smithers could now be moved to the non-existent department J9J, but his EmpID still could not be changed to 12: the key constraints remain even without referential constraints.

fields.Text: The instructor recommends you always {{c1::leave the referential constraints in}}, because they force you to follow the proper rules.

fields.Front: What does the slide's update_marks trigger do?
fields.Back: Before each update on the student marks table, for each row, it totals the marks, divides by five for the average, and sets the grade column to Excellent, Very Good, Good, Average or Not Promoted.

fields.Front: What does NEW refer to inside a trigger?
fields.Back: The new (current) row being worked on; the trigger runs like a loop over each affected row.

fields.Front: What is the slide's example of a constraint?
fields.Back: CREATE TABLE Persons (ID, LastName, FirstName, Age) with CHECK (Age >= 18): a state constraint checked on inserts and updates.

fields.Text: For the state constraint 'quantity ordered must be greater than 10', trying to enter {{c1::7}} gives an error, just as Access gave errors for key violations.

fields.Front: How does the instructor summarise the purpose of constraints?
fields.Back: Part of the beauty of the relational model: constraints make it really difficult to screw up your database by refusing weird values and values that do not relate to anything.

fields.Text: Insert <18, 'Flanders', 'Todd', 'P68', 'M'> 'looks like it should work' because 18 is {{c1::new and not null}}, but it fails because {{c2::department P68 does not exist}}.

fields.Front: Which four insert results does the instructor get in Access for the Lesson 10 employee table?
fields.Back: 13 Gumble: valid. 3 Granpa Simpson: duplicate key. NULL Ned Flanders: null key refused. 18 Todd Flanders in P68: related record required in Department (referential integrity).
